config.title: JWT Storage & Decode in React

intro.title: JWT Storage & Decode in React
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that securely stores a JSON Web Token (JWT) in the browser's localStorage and decodes it to display user information. You'll learn the core concept of handling authentication tokens in a client-side application, including safe storage and data extraction. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript, the jwt-decode library for parsing the token, and React hooks like useState to manage the token state. By the end, you'll understand how to retrieve, store, and use a JWT to personalize a user interface in a beginner-friendly way.
intro.usecase: JWT storage and decoding is essential for user authentication in modern web applications. When users log into platforms like banking dashboards, e-commerce sites, or project management tools, their session data is securely stored as JWTs. Developers implement this pattern to maintain user login states across page refreshes while keeping sensitive information protected. In practice, you'll decode JWTs to display user-specific content like profile names in navigation bars or permission-based UI elements in admin panels.

objectives: Implement secure JWT storage using browser localStorage or sessionStorage
Construct a TypeScript interface to define the structure of decoded JWT payload data
Apply a JWT decoding utility to extract user information from tokens
Initialize React state to manage authentication status and user data
Integrate JWT storage and decoding logic into React component lifecycle methods
Manipulate application routing based on JWT authentication state
Configure conditional rendering of UI elements using decoded JWT payload data

steps.title: Import React, useState, and useEffect
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useEffect from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in multiple named exports from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple hooks from React
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React, useState, and useEffect here
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports for React core and essential hooks are added, enabling state management and side effects in the component.
successCriteria: React, useState, and useEffect are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing all three: React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'. Check your import statement syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: import React, useState, and useEffect from the 'react' package. Use the import statement with curly braces for named exports.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. Use TypeScript typing by specifying the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to add the return type annotation after the parentheses.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined with proper TypeScript typing and returns null.
successCriteria: A functional component named App exists with return type JSX.Element and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure the component is named App, has the return type JSX.Element, and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Check that you've created a function named App with the correct return type.

steps.title: Initialize state for JWT token
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use useState to declare a state variable named 'token' with an initial value of null and a type of string | null.
steps.hint: Remember to call useState with null as the initial value and explicitly type it as string | null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: state for user data
const [user, setUser] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a token state variable that can hold either a JWT string or null.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with null as initial value and typed as string | null, creating a token state variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to type the state as string | null and initialize it with null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use useState to create a state variable named 'token' with type string | null and initial value null.

steps.title: Initialize state for decoded token data
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'decodedToken' with type 'object | null' and initialize it to null.
steps.hint: Remember to use the useState hook you imported earlier. The syntax is similar to your token state but with a different type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: state for user data
const [user, setUser] = useState<{name: string} | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a state variable ready to store the decoded JWT payload data when you implement the decoding logic later.
successCriteria: The component contains a 'decodedToken' state variable declared with useState, typed as 'object | null', and initialized to null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your state variable is named 'decodedToken' and has the correct type 'object | null'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to use useState to create a state variable named 'decodedToken' with type 'object | null' and initial value null.

steps.title: Define function to store JWT in localStorage
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function named saveToken that takes a token parameter of type string, stores it in localStorage, and updates the token state.
steps.hint: Use localStorage.setItem to store the token with a key like 'jwtToken', then call setToken to update the state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A saveToken function is defined that persists the token to localStorage and updates the component's token state.
successCriteria: The saveToken function is defined with a token parameter, uses localStorage.setItem, and calls setToken.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining the saveToken function, but make sure it stores the token in localStorage and updates the token state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The saveToken function is missing or doesn't properly store the token in localStorage and update the state.

steps.title: Add useEffect to load token on mount
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, add a useEffect hook that loads the JWT token from localStorage when the component first mounts.
steps.hint: Use useEffect with an empty dependency array to run code only on mount. Inside the effect, call localStorage.getItem() with your token key.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook is added with an empty dependency array and contains code to load a token from localStorage.
successCriteria: useEffect is called with a function
localStorage.getItem() is used inside the effect
setToken is called with the retrieved value if it exists
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your useEffect has an empty dependency array and properly retrieves the token from localStorage.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useEffect hook isn't set up correctly. Remember to use useEffect with an empty dependency array and load the token from localStorage inside it.

steps.title: Create main JSX structure with token display
steps.instruction: Return JSX from your App component that conditionally renders based on the token state. When token is truthy, show a paragraph displaying the token; when token is falsy, show a paragraph indicating no token is stored.
steps.hint:
Use a ternary operator in your JSX to check if token exists. For example: {token ?

Token: {token}

:

No token stored

}
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns JSX with conditional rendering that displays the token when it exists, or a message when it doesn't.
successCriteria: The component returns JSX with a ternary operator that conditionally renders different paragraphs based on the token state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using a ternary operator to conditionally render based on the token state.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're returning JSX with conditional rendering that displays different content based on whether token has a value.

steps.title: Add input and button to save JWT token
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your App component, add a text input element and a button element. The button should have an onClick handler that calls the saveToken function.
steps.hint: Use an <input> element for text input and a <button> element. Remember to set the input's value to the token state and update it with onChange.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will include a text input field and a button that, when clicked, will trigger the saveToken function to store the JWT token.
successCriteria: The return statement contains an <input> element with value={token} and onChange handler, and a <button> element with onClick handler calling saveToken.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some elements, but make sure you have both an <input> with value={token} and onChange, and a <button> with onClick={saveToken}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input and button elements are missing or incorrectly implemented. Check that you've added both elements with the proper attributes and handlers.

steps.title: Add button to decode token and display payload
steps.instruction: Add a button that calls the decodeToken function when clicked, and display the decoded payload data below it.
steps.hint: Create a button with an onClick handler that calls decodeToken, then add a section to render the decodedToken state.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Decode Token' appears that triggers the decodeToken function when clicked, and the decoded token data is displayed in a formatted way below it.
successCriteria: Button with onClick handler calling decodeToken is added, and decodedToken state is conditionally rendered below it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you added both the button with onClick handler and the conditional rendering for decodedToken.
steps.feedbackWrong: The decode button or payload display is missing. Add a button that calls decodeToken and display the decodedToken state.
